[...] However, vaccination rates can vary across communities, and even in Massachusetts, pediatricians say more parents are becoming skeptical of vaccines.

Will we see additional cases?

More cases of measles are certainly possible, given the increasing numbers of cases in other states. The level of measles in the U.S. now is the highest in more than three decades.

But Kuritzkes said he would be surprised to see a local outbreak given Massachusetts’s relatively high vaccination rates.

Image 5: A bar graph comparing measles cases by vaccination status shows that 94% of cases are in unvaccinated or unknown individuals and 6% are in vaccinated individuals.

The vast majority of measles cases occur among unvaccinated individuals, highlighting the critical role of vaccination in preventing transmission. [...] These maps illustrate how measles patterns have shifted over time, from widespread epidemics before vaccination to the localized outbreaks seen today.

### Measles Before Vaccination: A Historical Perspective

Before the introduction of the measles vaccine in 1963, measles was a widespread and often severe disease in the United States (Hübschen et al., 2022). Historical records indicate that measles outbreaks were common and could result in significant mortality, particularly among children.
